1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Female patient, 79 years old, was admitted to our hospital on Day 0, for “recurrent fever for more than 3 months.” History of present illness: More than 3 months before admission (Day -103), she developed fever without an obvious precipitating factor, Tmax 39℃, accompanied by chills and rigors, and cough without sputum production, without chest tightness or chest pain, without dizziness or fatigue, without abdominal pain or diarrhea, without urinary frequency or urgency, and without discomfort such as joint pain or rash. She presented to Chongqing Army Special Medical Center (9.05-10.02). During hospitalization, blood routine (9.5): WBC 5.09×10^9/L, მონocyte percentage 14.9%, hemoglobin 92 g/L. Liver function: albumin 31.3 g/L, AST 40.3 U/L, LDH 726.1 U/L. Inflammatory markers: CRP 33.26 mg/L, PCT 0.05 ng/ml, IL-6 25.41 pg/mt, ESR 59 mm/h. EB-DNA: 2.45E+03 copies/mt; blood culture on 09.12 (reported positive at 24 h): methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus hominis. Blood mNGS on 09.13 suggested Klebsiella pneumoniae (sequence count: 5). Respiratory pathogen panel, TORCH, CMV-DNA, TB-SPOT, blood lipase, amylase, stool routine + occult blood were negative. HbA1c 9.20%. Autoantibody panel negative, ANA 1:100, anti-CCP and RF negative; 9 tumor markers: NSE 32.90 ng/mL, CEA 7.01 ng/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and whole abdomen (9.10): 1. Scattered patchy opacities in both lungs, inflammatory lesions considered possible; 2. Multiple calcified lymph nodes in both hila and mediastinum; 3. Enlargement of the left and right atria, multiple high-density opacities in the coronary artery course; 4. Pancreatic changes, chronic pancreatitis considered? Pancreatic duct stones with distal pancreatic duct obstruction and dilatation; 5. Changes at the duodenal papilla, duodenal papillary hypertrophy considered? Neoplasm to be excluded; 6. Chronic cholecystitis; 7. Small bilateral renal calculi. Echocardiography (09.12): trace tricuspid regurgitation. Trace aortic regurgitation. Reduced left ventricular diastolic function. Endoscopic ultrasonography (09.18): 1. Chronic pancreatitis? 2. Pancreatic duct stones with pancreatic duct dilatation. Whole-body PET-CT on 09.30: 1. Scattered abnormal density opacities in both lungs, with mildly increased FDG metabolism in some lesions, inflammatory lesions considered most likely; left lower lobe 0.7*1.1 cm (SUVmax: 2.03); 2. Increased FDG metabolism in the proximal bones of the extremities, L2 vertebral body, and sacral vertebrae, reactive functional enhancement considered possible; 3. Scattered lacunar cerebral infarctions in both cerebral hemispheres; cerebral atrophy; 4. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes in both hila and mediastinum, with increased FDG metabolism in some lesions, inflammatory hyperplasia considered most likely; largest 1.8*0.9 cm (SUVmax: 3.63); 5. Pancreatic changes, no abnormally increased FDG metabolism seen, chronic pancreatitis considered possible; 6. Bilateral renal calculi; 7. Increased PDG metabolism in the uterine body (SUVma: 4.2), inflammatory lesion considered possible. During hospitalization, the patient’s temperature fluctuated between 38-39.2℃, with fever mostly occurring in the afternoon, intermittent chills and rigors, accompanied by upper abdominal and presternal discomfort. She remained febrile despite anti-infective treatment with piperacillin-tazobactam, vancomycin, cefoperazone-sulbactam, and ornidazole. On Day -70, the anti-infective regimen was adjusted to imipenem-cilastatin + tigecycline. After discharge, the patient still had recurrent fever. Five days earlier (11.26), she presented to Anxi County Hospital. Blood routine (11.26): WBC 3.50×10^9/L, hemoglobin 80 g/L, platelet count 131×10^9/L; serum G test: 143.74↑; serum GM test and serum cryptococcal capsular antigen negative; blood routine 11.30: WBC 2.29×10^9/L, hemoglobin 59 g/L, platelet count 12×10^9/L; malaria parasites and dengue virus both negative. Chest + upper abdominal CT on 11.27: 1. Multiple nodules in both lungs. 2. Main pancreatic duct dilatation and high-density opacity in the pancreatic duct region, pancreatic duct stone considered possible; calcification to be excluded. 3. Multiple small bilateral renal calculi. 4. Small amount of ascites. She remained febrile after treatment with cefoperazone sodium/sulbactam sodium, fluconazole, and TPIAO to increase platelets, with intermittent chills and rigors, and came to our hospital for further diagnosis and treatment. She was admitted from the emergency department with the tentative diagnosis of “fever of unknown origin.” Since disease onset, mental status was fair, physical strength was fair, appetite and food intake were poor, sleep was fair, weight decreased by 5 kg over the past 3 months, and urination and defecation were normal. Past history: diabetes mellitus for 30 years, usually managed with insulin for blood glucose control. In 2024 (10.23-11.08), she was hospitalized in the Department of Respiratory Medicine of our hospital for “recurrent fever for more than 1 month.” Personal history, menstrual/marital/reproductive history, and family history were unremarkable. Physical examination on admission: T: 36.4℃, P: 86/min, R: 20/min, BP: 124/78 mmHg, SpO2 96%. Appeared apathetic and was poorly cooperative with the examination. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes throughout the body. Neck supple, without resistance. Coarse breath sounds in both lungs, no dry or moist rales heard. Regular heart rhythm, no pathologic murmur heard in any valve auscultation area, no pericardial friction rub. Abdomen flat and soft, refused palpation; abdominal examination was unsatisfactory. Liver and spleen were not palpable below the costal margin, no percussion tenderness over the liver or kidneys, bowel sounds normal. No edema in either lower extremity. Pathologic signs negative. After admission, relevant examinations were completed: three routine tests (hospital day 1): blood routine: WBC 2.6×10^9/L, neutrophil percentage (NEUT%) 77.0%, neutrophil count (NEUT#) 2.0×10^9/L, hemoglobin (HGB) 85 g/L, platelet count (PLT) 15×10^9/L. Urinalysis: occult blood 1+, no other abnormalities. Stool routine + fecal occult blood test: normal. Biochemistry: albumin (ALB) 28 g/L, total bilirubin (TBIL) 13.5 umol/l, direct bilirubin (DBIL) 9.3 umol/l, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 16 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 92 U/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 136 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 1238 U/L, triglycerides, urea (UREA) 5.2 mmol/l, creatinine (CREA) 78 umol/l, uric acid (UA) 483 umol/L, potassium (K) 3.20 mmol/l. Coagulation function: prothrombin time (PT) 60.2 s, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 88.4 s, thrombin time (TT) 22.0 s, fibrinogen (FIB) 1.42 g/L, antithrombin activity (AT:A) 44.9%, fibrin(ogen) degradation products (FDP) 2.44 mg/L, D-dimer (D-D) 1.13 mg/L. Inflammatory markers: procalcitonin 1.40 ng/mL, C-reactive protein 81.50 mg/L, ESR 16 mm/h. Ferritin (SF) >1500.0 Ug/l. Cardiac function: N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide 33710.00 Pg/ml, quantitative troponin I 1.682 ng/mL. Microbiology: EBV DNA: 2.45E+03 Copies/mL; EB antibodies negative. Two blood cultures negative. Six-item respiratory pathogen panel, SARS-CoV-2 RNA, interferon-gamma release assay for TB infection, Widal reaction, human cytomegalovirus DNA, and four-item Brucellosis antibody panel were all normal. Tumor marker: carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) 8.25 ng/mL. Immunology: cellular immunity: CD4 cell count 121/μl, CD8 cell count 207/μl, CD4/CD8 0.58, NK cell percentage 3.56%, NK cell count 14/μl, CD19 cell count 25/μl, CD45 cell count 386/μl. Humoral immunity: immunoglobulin G 16.20 g/L↑, immunoglobulin A 4.800 g/L↑, complement C3 0.70 g/L↓. Direct antiglobulin test positive (2+). Autoantibodies, anticardiolipin antibodies, and ANCA were all negative. (12.03) Echocardiography (EF 34%): 1. Decreased wall motion, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction; 2. Left atrial enlargement, trace mitral regurgitation; 3. Trace tricuspid regurgitation; 4. Increased echogenicity of the aortic valve with trivial regurgitation; 5. Reduced left ventricular systolic and diastolic function. (12.04) Superficial lymph node ultrasonography: no obvious enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral neck or bilateral axillae. (12.05) Whole-abdomen ultrasonography: mild fatty liver. Multiple hypoechoic lesions in the liver, focal fat distribution? Hemangioma? Thickened and rough gallbladder wall. Slightly hyperechoic mural lesion in the gallbladder, nature undetermined, polyp considered possible. Dilatation of the upper common bile duct, stone in the middle-upper segment. Hyperechoic focus in the spleen, calcified plaque considered. Increased echogenicity of bilateral renal parenchyma. Multiple calculi in both kidneys. Rough bladder wall. Endometrial thickening. Ascites. Preliminary diagnoses: 1. Fever of unknown origin (infectious? neoplastic?); 2. Cause of pancytopenia to be investigated; 3. Cardiac insufficiency; 4. Coagulation dysfunction; 5. Hypoproteinemia; 6. Electrolyte disturbance; 7. Diabetes mellitus. Initial treatment: after admission, TPIAO was given to increase platelets, with supportive treatment including platelet and plasma transfusion.

differential_diagnoses.name: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)/macrophage activation syndrome
supporting_evidence: Recurrent high fever for more than 3 months; during hospitalization, body temperature fluctuated between 38-39.2°C, with fever occurring mostly in the afternoon, and intermittent chills and rigors.

Progressive pancytopenia: on 11.30, white blood cell count 2.29×10^9/L, hemoglobin 59 g/L, platelet count 12×10^9/L; after admission, white blood cell count 2.6×10^9/L, hemoglobin 85 g/L, platelet count 15×10^9/L
Ferritin >1500.0 ug/L markedly elevated
LDH markedly elevated: previously 726.1 U/L, 1238 U/L after admission
Markedly abnormal coagulation tests: PT 60.2s, APTT 88.4s, FIB 1.42g/L, AT activity 44.9%
Epstein-Barr virus DNA 2.45E+03 copies/mL, which may serve as one of the clues associated with secondary HLH
Weight loss of 5 kg, mental status fair, suggesting systemic inflammation/hypermetabolic state
Recurrent fever persisted after broad-spectrum antimicrobial and antifungal therapy, which is not consistent with the presentation of a simple common bacterial infection
opposing_evidence: No clear evidence of splenomegaly was provided in the first-stage information. On physical examination, the liver and spleen were not palpable below the costal margin. Abdominal ultrasound showed only a hyperechoic focus in the spleen, considered a calcified lesion.
Stage 1 information did not provide a triglyceride value
The first-stage information did not provide evidence of hemophagocytic cells in the bone marrow

differential_diagnoses.name: Hematologic malignancy (lymphoma, leukemia, or bone marrow infiltrative disease)
supporting_evidence: Elderly female, recurrent fever for more than 3 months, accompanied by a 5 kg weight loss over the past 3 months
Progressive pancytopenia suggests possible bone marrow involvement or a bone marrow failure/infiltrative disorder.
LDH was markedly elevated (from 726.1 U/L to 1238 U/L), suggesting high cellular turnover or tissue injury.

PET-CT showed increased FDG metabolism in the proximal bones of the extremities, the L2 vertebral body, and the sacral vertebrae; although the report favored reactive functional hyperactivity, bone marrow involvement still warrants caution
Multiple enlarged lymph nodes in both hilar regions and the mediastinum, some with increased FDG uptake
CD4, CD19, and NK cell counts were all low, suggesting an abnormal immune cell profile
Antiglobulin test positive (2+), which can be seen in immune abnormalities associated with some lymphoproliferative disorders
opposing_evidence: Color Doppler ultrasound of the superficial lymph nodes showed no significantly enlarged lymph nodes; on physical examination, there was no enlargement of superficial lymph nodes throughout the body.
PET-CT findings of the hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and pulmonary lesions are more suggestive of inflammatory hyperplasia/inflammatory lesions.
No information was provided in the first stage regarding peripheral blood blasts, bone marrow examination, or definite evidence of hepatosplenomegaly.

differential_diagnoses.name: Biliary tract infection/obstructive cholangitis or occult infection of the hepatobiliary-pancreatic system
supporting_evidence: During the course of the illness, the patient had upper abdominal discomfort; the abdominal examination was unsatisfactory because the patient refused palpation.
Imaging suggests chronic cholecystitis, thickened and irregular gallbladder wall, dilation of the upper common bile duct, and stones in the middle and upper common bile duct.
Whole-abdomen color Doppler ultrasound showed ascites, supporting the possibility of active disease in the abdominal cavity/hepatobiliary system.
Mild abnormalities in ALP 136 U/L and DBIL 9.3 umol/L, suggesting possible cholestasis/biliary involvement

Prior chest and abdominal CT showed pancreatic duct calculi with distal pancreatic duct obstruction and dilatation; a neoplasm at the duodenal papilla remains to be ruled out. All of these may cause biliary and pancreatic drainage obstruction and secondary infection.
Diabetes is a risk factor for severe biliary tract infection
opposing_evidence: ALT 16 U/L, TBIL 13.5 umol/L, no obvious jaundice-related biochemical abnormalities
Physical examination did not clearly demonstrate right upper quadrant tenderness, Murphy's sign, or percussion tenderness over the liver.
The fever persisted for more than 3 months and was unresponsive to multiple anti-infective treatments; biliary tract infection alone cannot fully explain all of the manifestations.

differential_diagnoses.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection (pulmonary tuberculosis or disseminated tuberculosis)
supporting_evidence: Elderly patient, long-term recurrent fever, 5 kg weight loss, poor appetite
Repeated chest imaging showed scattered patchy opacities/multiple nodules in both lungs
Multiple calcified lymph nodes in the bilateral hila and mediastinum, suggesting possible prior TB infection, with a possibility of reactivation in elderly and immunocompromised states
Increased FDG metabolism in some hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, which can be seen in chronic infections such as TB
Immunocompromise may lead to false-negative TB-related test results
opposing_evidence: TB-SPOT/tuberculosis infection T-cell interferon-gamma release assay normal
PET-CT findings in the lungs and lymph nodes are more suggestive of inflammatory lesions rather than specific TB manifestations.
In the first-stage information, no supporting evidence such as cough with sputum, cavitation, pleural effusion, or sputum acid-fast bacilli was provided.

stage2_input.text: Day +2 (hospital day 3): The patient developed recurrent hypoglycemia and hyponatremia. Cortisol-8AM 72.39 nmol/L↓, cortisol-4PM 62.46 nmol/L, ACTH 1.52 pg/mL↓. Thyroid function: TSH 0.10 mIU/L↓, FT3 3.23 pmol/L↓. Day +11 (hospital day 12): Fever developed, Tmax 40℃, accompanied by left flank pain. Urinalysis: WBC 6058.8/μl, RBC 427.7/μl, bacteria 10278/μl. 12-16 urine culture: Enterococcus faecalis, carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae. Day +14 (hospital day 15): Repeat chest CT showed that the left lower lobe nodule had enlarged significantly compared with before (2.4 cm×1.7 cm), with multiple new nodules in both lungs, some possibly MT. Whole-abdomen color Doppler ultrasound: mild fatty liver, thickened gallbladder wall, dilatation of the upper common bile duct with stones, multiple bilateral renal calculi, ascites. Contrast-enhanced chest CT: Multiple scattered nodular lesions in both lungs. A larger nodular lesion (2.4 cm×1.7 cm) was seen in the lateral basal segment of the left lower lobe, with relatively clear margins, showing marked heterogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced scan, with adjacent pleural thickening. Multiple additional small nodules were seen in both lungs (largest approximately 0.6 cm×0.6 cm), with clear margins; some were visible on the mediastinal window and showed heterogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced scan. Scattered reticular, honeycomb-like, patchy, and linear increased-density opacities were seen in both lungs, with relatively clear margins. Wall thickening of some bronchi in both lungs was present, more pronounced in the right lung. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were seen in both hilar regions and the mediastinum, some with calcification (largest short-axis diameter approximately 1.0 cm). Mild bilateral pleural thickening and small bilateral pleural effusions were present. Calcified foci were seen in the aortic wall and coronary artery walls within the scanned field. Partial cortical discontinuity was seen in the axillary segment of the left 9th rib; the T7 vertebral body was flattened and wedge-shaped. Scattered punctate calcifications were seen in both breasts, and scattered small punctate hyperdense foci were seen in both kidneys. The thyroid showed heterogeneous density, with nodular slightly low-density lesions within it. Multiple round low-density lesions were seen in the liver (largest diameter approximately 2.2 cm), some showing mild enhancement. One nodule was seen in each adrenal gland (largest diameter approximately 1.1 cm), showing mild enhancement on contrast-enhanced scan. Small-volume ascites.

differential_diagnoses.name: active tuberculosis
evidence: Multiple calcified foci throughout the body (lungs, pancreas, lymph nodes)
exclusion_reasons: Stable calcified lesion does not support active TB

differential_diagnoses.name: Sheehan syndrome
evidence: Simultaneous decreases in cortisol and ACTH suggest secondary adrenocortical insufficiency
exclusion_reasons: This syndrome is most commonly seen after massive postpartum hemorrhage; the 79-year-old woman had no relevant history.
No abnormalities were seen on pituitary MRI

differential_diagnoses.name: Disseminated cryptococcosis
evidence: Imaging may show multiple nodules, which may involve the lungs and central nervous system and cause endocrine abnormalities (pituitary involvement).
exclusion_reasons: Cryptococcal capsular antigen negative, not supportive

differential_diagnoses.name: NTM (nontuberculous mycobacterial) infection
evidence: May present with pulmonary nodules, lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, and resistance to conventional anti-TB drugs
exclusion_reasons: The disease course is usually longer and does not progress this rapidly.

differential_diagnoses.name: Invasive fungal disease
evidence: The patient has diabetes mellitus, long-term use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, and impaired cellular immunity (CD4 only 121/μl), and is in a high-risk population for fungal infection.
exclusion_reasons: Fluconazole treatment was ineffective, and the rate of lesion progression was not consistent with the characteristics of fungal infection

differential_diagnoses.name: Drug-induced thrombocytopenia
evidence: At an outside hospital, β-lactam antibiotics such as piperacillin/tazobactam had previously been used
exclusion_reasons: No improvement after discontinuation of the medication, not supporting a drug-related cause

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: CSF routine analysis: mildly bloody, light red, Pandy's test positive, RBC 22900×10^6/L, WBC 67×10^6/L (mononuclear cells 57%, multinuclear cells 43%)
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In the setting of prolonged fever, immunosuppression, altered mental status, and after lumbar puncture has been performed, routine cerebrospinal fluid analysis is used to determine whether a central nervous system inflammatory response is present. Information such as elevated white blood cells and differential count, and a positive Pandy test, helps support meningitis and distinguish whether it is predominantly infectious or caused by other etiologies; mild bloody contamination also suggests that puncture-related trauma, hemorrhage, or meningeal involvement should be considered in an integrated assessment. This examination can provide basic differential diagnostic clues for tuberculous meningitis, pyogenic meningitis, fungal meningitis, and neoplastic meningeal disease, and influences whether to continue intensified pathogen testing and empiric therapy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: CSF biochemistry: glucose 5.82 mmol/L, chloride 109 mmol/L, ADA 3.50 U/L, total protein 2243 mg/L
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has possible prolonged high fever, immunosuppression, and intracranial infection; cerebrospinal fluid biochemistry is an important component in determining the nature of meningitis. Markedly elevated total protein suggests blood-brain barrier disruption or inflammatory meningeal changes; glucose should be interpreted together with the simultaneous blood glucose level to determine whether there is a relative decrease, thereby helping differentiate among different etiologies such as TB, fungal, and bacterial causes; although ADA and chloride are not absolutely specific, they still have reference value for evaluating tuberculous meningitis. The purpose of this test is to further confirm the extent of meningeal involvement, improve recognition of chronic meningitis such as tuberculous meningitis, and provide a basis for whether to implement diagnostic anti-TB treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: India ink stain negative for Cryptococcus
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has a long history of diabetes mellitus, markedly impaired cellular immunity, previously elevated G test, progression of multiple pulmonary nodules, and prolonged persistent fever, placing the patient in a high-risk group for opportunistic infections; meanwhile, when the central nervous system is involved, cryptococcal meningitis must be a key focus of evaluation. India ink staining is an important rapid screening method for cerebrospinal fluid Cryptococcus after lumbar puncture. Although the cryptococcal capsular antigen was previously negative, direct testing of the cerebrospinal fluid is still required when clinical suspicion is high. This test is mainly used to promptly exclude or support cryptococcal meningitis, avoid missing a treatable fungal central nervous system infection, and affect whether subsequent antifungal therapy is needed.

The patient has a 30-year history of diabetes mellitus and also developed recurrent hypoglycemia during hospitalization, with marked blood glucose fluctuations. Interpretation of CSF glucose must be made in conjunction with the simultaneous blood glucose level. Simultaneous blood glucose is used to determine whether CSF glucose is relatively decreased, thereby improving the accuracy of assessing tuberculous, fungal, or bacterial meningitis and avoiding misinterpretation based solely on the absolute CSF glucose value. This test can also provide a reference for metabolic assessment during infection and for the safety of subsequent treatment.

recommended_exams.exam: Brain MRI without and with contrast
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Plain and contrast-enhanced brain MRI suggests possible meningitis
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has persistent fever and apathy, and in the setting of difficulty differentiating between systemic infection and neoplastic disease, has developed clues suggesting central nervous system involvement, requiring imaging evaluation of the meninges, brain parenchyma, and complications. Brain MRI, especially contrast-enhanced imaging, is more sensitive for meningeal enhancement, parenchymal lesions, cerebral infarction, and subdural effusion, and can help identify changes of meningitis and assess whether there are common complications of tuberculous meningitis or other intracranial lesions. The clinical objective of this examination is to further support the diagnosis of meningitis, evaluate for neoplastic meningeal involvement and other intracranial organic lesions, and provide imaging evidence for interpretation of lumbar puncture results and selection of the treatment plan.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Day +25 to 12-31: The patient's platelet count continued to decrease repeatedly
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: At the time of admission, the patient already had severe thrombocytopenia (15×10^9/L) and markedly abnormal coagulation function; subsequently, the counts continued to decline repeatedly and gradually manifested as pancytopenia. Dynamic monitoring of the platelet count is used, on the one hand, to assess disease progression and bleeding risk, especially for safety assessment before and after invasive procedures such as lumbar puncture and bone marrow aspiration; on the other hand, a persistent progressive decline suggests that infection alone or drug-related factors are difficult to explain, and more strongly supports bone marrow suppression, bone marrow infiltration, HLH, or a hematologic malignancy. This test directly affects transfusion support, whether further invasive examinations can be performed, and the subsequent choice of treatment intensity.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Atypical lymphocytes seen on blood smear
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has prolonged high fever, weight loss, markedly elevated LDH, elevated ferritin, pancytopenia, and repeated anti-infective treatment has been ineffective, which already strongly suggests a hematologic malignancy or HLH. A peripheral blood smear can rapidly assess for abnormal lymphocytes, blasts, or other morphologic evidence suggestive of bone marrow infiltration/lymphoproliferative disease. This test helps shift the diagnostic focus from infectious fever to hematologic malignancy, determine whether bone marrow aspiration pathology and further subclassification studies should be performed as soon as possible, and provide direct clues to explain the cause of the pancytopenia.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Day +30 (hospital day 31): Bone marrow aspiration was performed, and the results suggested lymphoma.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has persistent high fever, marked wasting, progressive pancytopenia, abnormal lymphocytes on peripheral blood smear, markedly elevated LDH and ferritin, and coagulation abnormalities; HLH and a hematologic malignancy had already been highly suspected in the earlier stage. Bone marrow aspiration is the key examination to determine whether the pancytopenia is caused by bone marrow infiltration, abnormal proliferation, or hemophagocytosis, and it allows direct observation of the proportion and morphology of abnormal cells. The main clinical purpose of this examination is to confirm whether there is bone marrow involvement by lymphoma/leukemia, explain the underlying cause of fever and cytopenias, and provide critical evidence for subsequent pathologic classification, prognostic assessment, and whether to proceed with antineoplastic treatment in the hematology department.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bone marrow aspiration pathology: active bone marrow hyperplasia, with extensive infiltration by abnormal lymphocytes; the cells vary in size, with coarse nuclear chromatin and visible nucleoli; the normal three hematopoietic lineages are suppressed
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Based on abnormal findings on bone marrow aspiration, bone marrow pathology is the निर्णसive examination for further confirming the nature of the lesion. The patient's prior clinical manifestations were complex, including prolonged fever and multiple pulmonary nodules, as well as a tendency toward HLH and progressive pancytopenia; infection or immune abnormalities alone were insufficient to fully explain the presentation. By evaluating bone marrow architecture, the degree of abnormal lymphocytic infiltration, and suppression of the normal three hematopoietic lineages, bone marrow pathology can determine whether there is bone marrow infiltration by lymphoma and distinguish it from reactive hyperplasia, infection-related changes, and other conditions. This examination plays a critical role in the final diagnosis, assessment of the extent of bone marrow involvement, promotion of subsequent immunohistochemical subtyping, and formulation of treatment strategies such as chemotherapy/palliation.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Day +18 (hospital day 19): Lumbar puncture was completed. CSF routine analysis: mildly bloody, light red color, Pandy test positive, RBC 22900×10^6/L, WBC 67×10^6/L (mononuclear cells 57%, multinuclear cells 43%). CSF biochemistry: glucose 5.82 mmol/L, chloride 109 mmol/L, ADA 3.50 U/L, total protein 2243 mg/L. India ink stain did not detect Cryptococcus. Simultaneous blood glucose 14.50 mmol/L. Plain and contrast-enhanced brain MRI suggested possible meningitis: a small punctate DWI hyperintense signal was seen in the left parietal lobe (possible acute-subacute cerebral infarction); multiple punctate and patchy long T1 and long T2 signals were seen in the bilateral centrum semiovale and basal ganglia regions, with some lesions showing slightly hyperintense signal on T2-FLAIR, and some distributed in a periventricular halo pattern; no enhancement was seen on contrast-enhanced imaging. Small amount of bilateral frontoparietal subdural effusion (width approximately 0.8 cm). Contrast-enhanced imaging showed obvious linear enhancement of the bilateral meninges, consistent with meningitic changes; no obvious abnormal enhancing lesion was seen in the brain parenchyma. Partial widening of the ventricles, sulci, and cisterns was present, and the midline brain structures were centered. Day +25 to 12-31: The patient's platelet count continued to decrease recurrently, with pancytopenia, and abnormal lymphocytes were seen on peripheral blood smear. Day +30 (hospital day 31): Bone marrow aspiration was completed, and the result suggested lymphoma. Bone marrow aspiration pathology: active bone marrow hyperplasia with extensive infiltration by abnormal lymphocytes of varying cell size; coarse nuclear chromatin and visible nucleoli; suppression of the normal three hematopoietic lineages.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Lymphoma (pathologic subtype pending immunohistochemistry); hemophagocytic syndrome (highly suspected); tuberculous meningitis (highly suspected); multiple organ dysfunction; urinary tract infection (CRKP); secondary adrenal insufficiency; diabetes mellitus; effusions in multiple serous cavities.

Normal trilineage hematopoiesis is suppressed. Pathologic diagnosis: bone marrow infiltration by lymphoma

treatment_plan: Diagnostic anti-TB treatment: methylprednisolone 40mg→80mg; isoniazid 300mg qd; rifampin 0.45g qd; pyrazinamide 0.5g bid; ethambutol 0.75g→0.6g qd; amikacin 600mg qd; levofloxacin 0.5g qd
Intravenous human immunoglobulin 15 g qd (12-25 to 12-29) for immune modulation
treatment_response: During anti-TB treatment, liver function impairment occurred; isoniazid and rifampin were discontinued, and levofloxacin and amikacin were added.
The patient's platelet count remained repeatedly decreased, with trilineage cytopenia.
After the patient's family was informed of the condition, they declined further treatment, including chemotherapy in Hematology, requested discharge, and discharge was processed.
